subject: Cloud Computing
title: Supply Chain Attacks on Cloud
description: A quick win: understand Supply Chain Attacks on Cloud.

hook.text: SolarWinds was trusted by 18,000 organizations. Attackers poisoned its software update — and got inside all of them.

buildup.text: Supply chain attacks compromise a trusted vendor, then use that trust to reach their real targets.

discovery.text: Cloud environments are built on layers of third-party software: libraries, containers, and managed services.

twist.text: You might trust your code. But do you trust every open-source dependency your code relies on?

climax.text: Supply chain security requires scanning dependencies, verifying signatures, and limiting trust boundaries.

punchline.text: You're only as secure as your weakest dependency.

quiz.question: What made the SolarWinds attack so devastating?
options: Attackers compromised a trusted software update that 18,000 organizations installed
SolarWinds accidentally deleted all customer data
A data center fire destroyed SolarWinds' backup systems

details.summary: Supply chain attacks compromise trusted third-party software, libraries, or services to infiltrate cloud environments indirectly. The SolarWinds attack demonstrated how a single compromised update could grant attackers access to thousands of organizations.
details.whyItMatters: Modern cloud deployments depend on hundreds of third-party components. A single compromised dependency can bypass all direct security controls and affect organizations globally.
takeaways: SolarWinds showed supply chain risk at massive scale
Software bill of materials helps track dependencies

faq.question: How can organizations protect against supply chain attacks?
faq.answer: Maintain a software bill of materials, scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities, verify signatures on packages, use private registries for critical dependencies, and implement runtime monitoring that detects unexpected behavior from trusted components.

faq.question: What was the SolarWinds attack?
faq.answer: Attackers inserted malicious code into a SolarWinds software update distributed to around 18,000 organizations. The compromised update gave attackers backdoor access to government agencies and major corporations, remaining undetected for months.
